actions.name: Repeated movement testing in extension (symptom response over several reps)

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes the X-ray showing 'mild degenerative disc changes' means his spine is seriously deteriorating or falling apart, and that bending could cause permanent damage.
mismatches.recordEvidence: X-ray report actually states mild degenerative disc narrowing only at L4-L5, no fracture, no destructive lesion, no spondylolisthesis - a common, often age-related finding not indicative of structural failure.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Imaging findings described as 'degenerative' are frequently normal age-related changes and poorly correlate with pain severity or prognosis; clear reassurance and reframing of imaging language is a key part of reducing fear-avoidance and catastrophizing.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports he has been resting in bed and avoiding all bending because he fears movement will cause further injury.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Urgent care note documents a normal neurologic exam (5/5 strength, intact sensation, symmetric reflexes, negative SLR) at the time of injury, indicating no evidence supporting a need for strict bed rest or activity avoidance.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Prolonged bed rest and activity avoidance are not supported by exam findings and are associated with worse outcomes in acute non-specific low back pain; early return to normal activity and movement is evidence-based.

objectives.text: Perform a thorough red flag screen to rule out serious spinal pathology (cauda equina, fracture, infection, malignancy) before proceeding with mechanical evaluation.
Use patient-guided repeated movement testing (flexion, extension, side-bending, SLR) via video to classify the directional preference and mechanical pattern of the low back pain.
Identify and address fear-avoidance beliefs and catastrophizing stemming from misinterpretation of imaging language, and reframe benign degenerative findings appropriately.
Integrate psychosocial and occupational context (job security fears, physical job demands, disability questionnaire) into the plan of care and prognosis.
Recognize and correctly respond to a patient-record mismatch regarding imaging interpretation and activity restriction, communicating findings in a way that reduces fear rather than reinforcing it.

Formulate an appropriate PT diagnosis, prognosis, and graded exercise plan of care emphasizing extension-biased movement, education, and graded return to work, without ordering or requesting MRI outside PT scope.

patient.name: Luis Herrera
patient.appearance: A sturdily built man in his mid-40s with short dark hair, visible on camera wearing a gray t-shirt, sitting carefully upright on the edge of a couch in a modestly furnished living room with a visible back brace on the armrest nearby. His expression is earnest and a bit tense, shifting position occasionally as if uncomfortable.

persona.communicationStyle: Direct and respectful, sometimes downplays fear until asked directly, uses plain non-medical language.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious about his job and worried his back is seriously damaged, eager for reassurance or a definitive scan.

He and his wife, who works part-time, are raising two children in Allentown, Pennsylvania. He takes pride in being a reliable provider and rarely misses work.

Confusion about whether bending or moving will make his back worse

scenario.studentBrief: You are the physical therapy student seeing Luis Herrera, a 44-year-old warehouse worker, for an initial telehealth evaluation of low back pain that started 3 weeks ago after a lifting injury at work. He was seen at urgent care, given an X-ray, and referred to PT. Conduct a focused history and remote movement-based examination and begin formulating a plan of care.

profile.summary: "This case portrays a 44-year-old warehouse worker with acute non-specific low back pain and a directional preference toward extension, complicated by fear-avoidance behavior and catastrophizing driven by misinterpretation of 'degenerative' imaging language. It teaches PT students to screen red flags via telehealth, perform camera-guided mechanical movement testing, identify a patient-chart mismatch around imaging beliefs and activity avoidance, and build a biopsychosocially-informed plan of care emphasizing education and graded exercise rather than imaging or passive rest."
profile.title: "Fear-Avoidant Acute Low Back Pain with Extension Directional Preference in a Warehouse Worker"

answerKey.primaryProblem: Acute non-specific (mechanical) low back pain with extension directional preference and significant fear-avoidance/catastrophizing behavior, in the setting of benign age-related degenerative imaging findings
differential: Mechanical/discogenic low back pain with directional preference (most consistent with findings)
Lumbar facet or sacroiliac referred pain (less likely given clear directional preference and centralization)
Lumbar radiculopathy/disc herniation with nerve root involvement (ruled out: negative SLR, no dermatomal symptoms, normal strength/sensation)
Cauda equina syndrome (ruled out: no saddle anesthesia, no bowel/bladder dysfunction, no bilateral leg weakness)
Spinal fracture, infection, or malignancy (ruled out: no trauma beyond lifting, no fever, no weight loss, no cancer history, X-ray without fracture or destructive lesion)
keyFindings: 3 weeks of central/right-sided low back pain after a lifting injury, worse with flexion and sitting, eased by walking and extension
Repeated extension testing reduces pain from 6/10 to 3/10 without peripheralization, indicating an extension-biased directional preference
Negative bilateral straight leg raise, normal strength/sensation/reflex screen, no red flag symptoms on history
ODI 38% (moderate disability), driven by lifting, sitting, and standing limitations
Significant fear-avoidance and catastrophizing beliefs stemming from misinterpretation of 'mild degenerative disc changes' on X-ray, leading to bed rest and continuous back belt use

Mismatch: patient believes imaging shows serious spinal deterioration and avoids all bending, but the X-ray and urgent care exam show benign findings and a normal neurologic exam not supporting bed rest
plan: Provide clear, reassuring education reframing the X-ray finding of 'mild degenerative disc changes' as a common, often age-related finding not indicative of structural failure or impending paralysis
Counsel against prolonged bed rest and continuous back belt use; encourage gradual resumption of normal movement and activity as tolerated

Initiate an extension-biased home exercise program (e.g., prone press-ups/McKenzie extension progressions) based on positive response to repeated extension testing, with close monitoring for any peripheralization
Address fear-avoidance beliefs directly using graded exposure to bending-type movements and pain neuroscience education
Collaborate on a graded, criterion-based return-to-work plan with the employer light-duty restriction, progressing lifting tolerance over several weeks rather than fixed calendar deadline

Reassess ODI and movement findings at follow-up visits to track progress; no indication at this time for MRI or referral back to physician given reassuring red flag screen and clear mechanical presentation
Educate that if red flag symptoms (saddle numbness, bowel/bladder changes, bilateral leg weakness/numbness, fever, unexplained weight loss) develop, prompt medical referral is needed
redFlags: Bowel or bladder incontinence or retention
Bilateral lower extremity weakness or numbness
Unexplained weight loss or history of cancer
educationPoints: Degenerative disc findings on imaging are extremely common with age and poorly correlate with pain or disability; language used to describe imaging can strongly influence patient fear and behavior
Prolonged bed rest and activity avoidance worsen outcomes in acute non-specific low back pain; early, graded return to movement is evidence-based

Directional preference testing (repeated movements) is a valid, low-cost tool to guide exercise selection in mechanical low back pain, feasible via telehealth with patient self-report of symptom response
A thorough red flag screen can be performed effectively through history alone in a telehealth visit when access to in-person neurologic testing is limited
Addressing fear-avoidance beliefs and job-related psychosocial stressors is essential to functional recovery and should be integrated into the plan of care alongside exercise prescription
